title: Drawing balls from urns
objectives: Solve urn puzzles with a symmetry argument.

screens.title: The last ball
screens.prose: An urn holds five red and three blue balls. You draw them all, one at a time, without putting any back. Slide through some shuffles and watch the last place.

state.caption: Five red (R) and three blue (B) balls. Slide to draw them all out in a random order.

screens.question: What is the chance the last ball drawn is red? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Is the last place any different from the first?
Before any draw, the first ball is red with chance $\tfrac58$.
Every place is alike, so the last is red with chance $\tfrac58$ too.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac58 = 0.625$, the same as for the first ball.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of the whole order as one shuffle of eight balls.

byKey.half: You gave red and blue equal chances. There are five reds and only three blues.
byKey.blue: That is the chance the last ball is blue.

explain.text: Drawing them all out is just a random order of the eight balls. Each place is equally likely to hold any ball. So the last place is red with chance $\tfrac58$.

screens.title: Reds before the first blue
screens.prose: The same urn. In this order one red comes before the first blue. Other orders give 0, 2, 3, 4 or 5.

state.caption: One order: R B R R B R B R. One red comes before the first blue.

screens.question: On average, how many reds come before the first blue? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: The three blues cut the reds into gaps, as the aces did.
Three blues make four gaps.
Five reds over four gaps: $\tfrac54$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Share the five reds among the gaps the blues make.

byKey.three-gaps: You used three gaps. Three blues make four: before, between and after them.
byKey.share: That is the chance a ball is red. The question asks for a count.

explain.text: A red is equally likely to sit in any of four places among the blues. So it comes first with chance $\tfrac14$, and five reds give $\tfrac54$. This is the gap argument from the cards.

screens.title: Pólya’s urn
screens.prose: A new urn: one red, one blue. Draw a ball, then return it with one more of its colour. So reds breed reds. Fill in the chance of each path of two draws.

state.caption: Draw a ball, then put it back with one more of its colour.

screens.question: Fill in the four path chances, as fractions or to four decimal places.

hints.text: Multiply along each path.
Red then red is $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac23$.
$\tfrac13$, $\tfrac16$, $\tfrac16$, $\tfrac13$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the two branch chances on each path.

explain.text: Two reds have chance $\tfrac13$, one red $\tfrac16 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac13$, and no red $\tfrac13$. Each count of reds is equally likely.

screens.title: Four draws
screens.prose: Two draws gave 0, 1 or 2 reds, each with chance $\tfrac13$. The pattern holds for any number of draws: the count of reds is uniform.

state.caption: Reds in two draws from 1 R and 1 B: each count has chance $\tfrac13$.

screens.question: From one red and one blue, what is the chance of exactly two reds in four draws?

hints.text: How many counts are possible in four draws?
The count can be 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4.
Five counts, all equally likely: $\tfrac15$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the possible numbers of reds in four draws.

byKey.binomial: You used $\binom42 / 16$, as for fair coin flips. Pólya draws are not independent: early reds make later reds likelier.
byKey.third: You kept the two-draw answer. Four draws allow five counts.

explain.text: In $n$ draws the count of reds is uniform on $0, 1, \dots, n$. With four draws each count has chance $\tfrac15$. Any single path with two reds has chance $\tfrac1{30}$, and six such paths give $\tfrac15$.

screens.title: Are reds used up?
screens.prose: Back to five red and three blue, no replacement. You draw three balls but do not look at the first two.

state.caption: Three balls drawn. Nobody has looked at the first two.

screens.question: What is the chance the third ball is red?

options.text: Less than $\tfrac58$, because reds get used up
options.why: That is the blurted answer. Reds are used up only if you know some came out. Unseen draws change nothing.
You assumed two reds came out first. Nobody looked at them.
You gave red and blue equal weight. Five of the eight balls are red.

hints.text: What do you know about the first two balls?
Nothing: they were not looked at.
Every place is alike, so the third is red with chance $\tfrac58$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use symmetry: you know nothing about the first two.

byKey.b: You assumed reds were used up. That needs you to see them. With nothing seen, the third place is like the first.

explain.text: Reds are used up only if you see them leave. With the first two unseen, the third place is like any other. Its chance is $\tfrac58$.

screens.title: Symmetry
screens.prose:
Without replacement, every draw has the same chance before you look: the **symmetry** of the order. With $r$ red and $b$ blue,

$$P(\text{draw } k \text{ is red}) = \frac{r}{r + b}$$

$$E[\text{reds before first blue}] = \frac{r}{b + 1}$$
screens.question: Seven red and three blue balls. What is the chance the last ball is blue?

options.why: You removed a ball before the last draw. Nothing is seen, so the last place is like the first.
That is the chance the last ball is red.

hints.text: Is the last place special?
Use the first-draw chance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every place is alike.

explain.text: The last place is like the first. So it is blue with chance $\tfrac{3}{10}$.

screens.title: Why place 7 is like place 1
screens.prose: An interviewer asks you to justify the symmetry for five red and three blue balls. Put the argument in order.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Label the eight balls. Drawing them all gives a random order, each order equally likely.
Swap whatever sits in places 1 and 7. This matches the orders one to one.
An order with red in place 7 becomes one with red in place 1, and back.
So the two counts are equal: $P(\text{7th red}) = P(\text{1st red}) = \tfrac58$.
Draws without replacement are independent, so each is red with chance $\tfrac58$.

hints.text: Start with what makes the orders equally likely.
A swap of two places is a one-to-one map.
Orders, swap, what the swap does to red, conclusion.

feedback.correct: Equally likely orders, a swap, a one-to-one match, equal chances.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the random order, then use the swap.

byKey.d1: The draws are not independent: a red first makes a red second less likely. The swap argument needs no independence.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one about independence belongs.

explain.text: The swap pairs each order with red in place 7 with one with red in place 1. Equal counts give equal chances. The draws are dependent, yet each one alone has chance $\tfrac58$.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three new puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 9 in all. Keep your own time. Give each answer to four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: 6 white and 4 black balls, no replacement. Expected whites drawn before the first black?
The same urn. Chance the 7th ball drawn is black?
Pólya’s urn from 2 red and 1 blue. Chance the second draw is red?

hints.text: Gaps for the first, symmetry for the second and third.
Four blacks make five gaps for six whites.
$\tfrac65$; $\tfrac4{10}$; $\tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac34 + \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac24 = \tfrac23$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Check the first answer. Four blacks make five gaps, so $\tfrac65$.
byKey.r1c1: Check the second answer. The 7th place is like the first: $\tfrac4{10}$.
byKey.r2c1: Check the third answer. Split on the first draw: $\tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac34 + \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac24$.

explain.text: Whites before the first black: $\tfrac{6}{4 + 1} = 1.2$. The 7th draw is black with chance $\tfrac4{10}$. In Pólya’s urn the second draw is red with chance $\tfrac23$, the same as the first.

screens.title: Follow-up: a bigger urn
screens.prose: You answered 1.25 for five red and three blue. The interviewer changes the urn: ten red and four blue.
screens.question: On average, how many reds come before the first blue?

hints.text: Count the gaps the blues make.
Four blues make five gaps.

byKey.four-gaps: You used four gaps. Four blues make five.
byKey.ratio: That is the chance a ball is red. The question asks for a count.

explain.text: Each red is ahead of all four blues with chance $\tfrac15$. Ten reds give 2 on average. Saying the formula $r/(b + 1)$ first lets the interviewer check you.

screens.title: An audit sample
screens.prose: A book holds 200 trades, 12 of them with a booking error. An auditor checks trades one at a time, in random order, without repeats.

state.caption: Green: 188 clean trades. Orange: 12 trades with a booking error.

screens.question: How many clean trades does the auditor expect to check before finding the first error? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: The errors play the part of the blue balls.
12 errors make 13 gaps for 188 clean trades.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Share the clean trades among the gaps the errors make.

byKey.twelve-gaps: You used 12 gaps. Twelve errors make 13.
byKey.all: You divided all 200 trades by 12. Only the 188 clean trades sit in the gaps.

explain.text: The 12 errors cut the 188 clean trades into 13 gaps of equal mean. So about $14.46$ clean trades come first. By symmetry, the 5th trade checked is an error with chance $\tfrac{12}{200} = 0.06$, whatever came before unseen.

canvas.caption: 12 orange errors cut the 188 green clean trades into 13 gaps.

ideas: Drawing every ball gives a random order, so each place has the first-draw chance.
$b$ blue balls cut the reds into $b + 1$ gaps: $\tfrac{r}{b + 1}$ reds come first on average.
From one of each colour, Pólya’s red count after $n$ draws is uniform on $0$ to $n$.

formula.name: Any single draw
formula.note: True for every $k$ until you look.

summary.trap: Saying later draws are less likely to be red because reds get used up. That needs you to see them go.

quiz.prose: An urn holds five red balls and nothing else. You draw them all.
quiz.question: What is the chance the last ball drawn is red?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the urn holds.

byKey.fifth: You found the chance of one named ball. Any red ball will do, and all five are red.
byKey.half: There is no blue to compete with.

explain.text: With one colour, $\tfrac{r}{r + b} = \tfrac55 = 1$. The edge case is a useful check on any urn formula.

quiz.prose: Five red and three blue balls, drawn without replacement.
quiz.question: What is the chance the first and the last balls are both red? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat the first and last places as the first two draws.

byKey.square: You squared $\tfrac58$. Once the first ball is red, only 4 of the other 7 are red.

explain.text: By symmetry the first and last places act like the first two draws. So the chance is $\tfrac58 \times \tfrac47 = \tfrac5{14}$.

quiz.prose: Pólya’s urn from one red and one blue ball. You do not see the first two draws.
quiz.question: What is the chance the third draw is red?

options.text: More than $\tfrac12$, because reds breed reds
options.why: Blues breed blues just as fast. With nothing seen, the two colours stay alike.

options.text: It cannot be found without the first two draws
options.why: Average over what they might have been. By symmetry between colours, red has chance $\tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Red and blue start equal, and the rule treats them alike.

explain.text: The rule treats red and blue alike, and they start level. So every unseen draw is red with chance $\tfrac12$.
